PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 148 — Lesson 172: Endocrine, Renal & Metabolic Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate hormone axes, glucose regulation, kidney filtration, electrolytes, volume, medications, life stage, and organ-protection evidence to recognize emergencies, distinguish acute from chronic disease, choose focused testing, initiate safe care, and arrange appropriate monitoring or referral.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize hypoglycemia, DKA, HHS, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxedema coma, severe electrolyte disorders, obstruction, and kidney-related emergencies.
  • Interpret glucose and A1C, TSH and free T4, creatinine and eGFR, urine albumin, urinalysis, electrolytes, calcium, and acid-base patterns in context.
  • Differentiate type 1 and type 2 diabetes, primary and central endocrine disease, and acute kidney injury from chronic kidney disease.
  • Use cardiovascular, kidney, weight, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, and patient priorities to individualize metabolic treatment.
  • Distinguish lower urinary disease from pyelonephritis, obstruction, nephritic or nephrotic patterns, and noninfectious causes.
  • Adjust evaluation and treatment for children, pregnancy, older adults, frailty, and changing organ function.
  • Prevent medication-related endocrine, electrolyte, and kidney harm.
  • Define monitoring, referral, sick-day education, and return precautions.

Part 1 — Homeostasis Connects These Systems

Endocrine glands coordinate metabolism, stress response, growth, reproduction, calcium, and water balance. Kidneys regulate filtration, volume, potassium, acid-base status, erythropoietin, mineral metabolism, and drug clearance. Diabetes and hypertension injure kidneys; kidney disease changes glucose, insulin, electrolytes, and medication safety.

Do not study these as isolated organs. A patient with vomiting may develop prerenal AKI, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and medication accumulation simultaneously.

Part 2 — Stability Before Classification

Immediate threats include altered mentation, seizure, shock, severe dehydration, respiratory compensation or failure, arrhythmia, anuria, pulmonary edema, severe potassium disorder, hyperglycemic crisis, adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, and severe symptomatic calcium disturbance.

Obtain rapid glucose in unexplained neurologic change. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, perfusion, hydration, ECG when indicated, and medication exposure. Stabilization and emergency transfer take priority over outpatient endocrine refinement.

Part 3 — Diabetes Diagnosis Requires the Correct Context

ADA 2026 criteria for nonpregnant individuals include A1C at least 6.5%, fasting plasma glucose at least 126 mg/dL, two-hour plasma glucose at least 200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, or random plasma glucose at least 200 mg/dL with classic hyperglycemic symptoms or crisis.

Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, confirm the diagnosis with repeat or second abnormal testing. Pregnancy uses specific pathways. Red-cell turnover, hemoglobin variants, dialysis, pregnancy, and other conditions can make A1C discordant; use appropriate plasma glucose criteria.

Part 4 — Classify the Diabetes Phenotype

Age and body size alone do not prove type. Type 1 diabetes can occur in adults; type 2 can occur in youth. Consider tempo, ketosis, weight loss, autoimmune history, insulin resistance, family pattern, pancreatic disease, medications, and monogenic clues.

Misclassifying progressive insulin deficiency as routine type 2 diabetes can lead to DKA. When phenotype is uncertain, use appropriate antibody, C-peptide, genetic, or specialist evaluation rather than guessing from appearance.

Part 5 — Individualize Glycemic Goals

Balance microvascular benefit, cardiovascular and kidney benefit, hypoglycemia, treatment burden, life expectancy, cognition, pregnancy, comorbidity, cost, and patient priorities. A lower A1C is not automatically safer.

Assess glucose patterns rather than A1C alone. Recurrent hypoglycemia, wide variability, steroid exposure, anemia, or changing kidney function can make the average misleading.

Part 6 — Hypoglycemia Requires Immediate Action and Prevention

Symptoms include sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, confusion, behavior change, seizure, or loss of consciousness. ADA defines level 1 as glucose below 70 and at least 54 mg/dL, level 2 as below 54 mg/dL, and level 3 as severe cognitive or physical impairment requiring assistance regardless of measured value.

A conscious patient able to swallow receives fast-acting glucose according to the current plan and rechecks promptly. An unresponsive or unsafe-to-swallow patient needs glucagon or emergency treatment. Then identify insulin or secretagogue exposure, missed food, exercise, alcohol, kidney decline, weight change, food insecurity, or dosing error and modify the regimen.

Part 7 — DKA and HHS Are Emergencies

DKA combines insulin deficiency, ketone production, metabolic acidosis, osmotic diuresis, and electrolyte loss. HHS features profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with severe dehydration and variable ketosis. Overlap occurs.

Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep respirations, dehydration, weakness, and cognitive change are warning signs. Serum potassium may appear normal or high despite total-body depletion. Management requires emergency fluid, electrolyte, insulin, and precipitant treatment with close monitoring.

Part 8 — Sick-Day Planning Prevents Crisis

Illness can increase glucose and ketones even when intake falls. Patients using insulin need individualized instructions for glucose and ketone checks, hydration, carbohydrate intake, medication continuation or temporary holding, and when to call or seek emergency care.

Do not advise a person with type 1 diabetes to stop basal insulin simply because they are not eating. Some noninsulin medicines may need temporary interruption during dehydration, fasting, surgery, or acute illness under a specific plan.

Part 9 — Select Therapy by Comorbidity and Risk

For type 2 diabetes, consider atherosclerotic disease, heart failure, CKD, obesity, hypoglycemia risk, kidney function, adverse effects, cost, access, and patient preference—not A1C alone. Some agents provide cardiorenal benefit beyond glucose lowering.

Insulin is appropriate when insulin deficiency, marked symptomatic hyperglycemia, catabolism, pregnancy context, acute illness, or other circumstances require it. Verify technique, storage, dosing, monitoring, and hypoglycemia preparedness.

Part 10 — Diabetes Complication Review

Assess blood pressure, lipids, tobacco, kidney function and albuminuria, retinal screening, neuropathy, foot skin and pulses, dental health, vaccination, mental health, and treatment access. New visual change, infected ulcer, ischemia, or progressive kidney disease requires timely action.

Prevention is longitudinal. A normal prior screen does not explain a new symptom.

Part 11 — The Thyroid Axis

In primary hypothyroidism, thyroid failure lowers free T4 and removes negative feedback, raising TSH. In primary hyperthyroidism, thyroid hormone rises and suppresses TSH. Central pituitary or hypothalamic disease can produce low free T4 with an inappropriately low or normal TSH.

Pregnancy, severe illness, biotin, medications, assay interference, and timing affect results. Interpret TSH and free T4 as an axis rather than labeling a patient from one value.

Part 12 — Hypothyroidism

Symptoms can include fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight change, bradycardia, menstrual or fertility change, slowed cognition, and myalgias. They are nonspecific, so confirm biochemically and consider anemia, sleep disorder, depression, medication effect, and other mimics.

Levothyroxine is standard replacement for most patients. Dose and monitoring depend on age, body factors, cardiac disease, pregnancy, cause, adherence, interactions, and absorption. Recheck only after sufficient time for steady-state response unless urgency or pregnancy guidance requires otherwise.

Part 13 — Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis

Symptoms include heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, anxiety, insomnia, frequent stools, muscle weakness, tachycardia, palpitations, and atrial fibrillation. Distinguish increased hormone synthesis from thyroiditis or exogenous hormone because treatment differs.

Evaluate severity, pregnancy, cardiovascular status, eye findings, goiter or nodules, medication exposure, and etiology. Antithyroid therapy, radioactive iodine, surgery, beta blockade, and observation are not interchangeable across causes and life stages.

Part 14 — Thyroid Emergencies

Thyroid storm is severe decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever, marked tachycardia or arrhythmia, CNS dysfunction, heart failure, and GI or hepatic manifestations. Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroid decompensation with altered mentation, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, and shock.

Both require emergency hospitalization and empiric management guided by current protocol. Do not wait for a single confirmatory test when the clinical syndrome is life-threatening.

Part 15 — Thyroid Nodules

Assess radiation history, family history, growth, hoarseness, dysphagia, neck nodes, compressive symptoms, and hyperthyroid symptoms. Begin with TSH and appropriate ultrasound characterization; functional imaging and biopsy decisions depend on TSH and sonographic risk.

A suppressed TSH changes the pathway. Rapid growth, fixation, abnormal nodes, vocal change, or airway symptoms require expedited evaluation. Do not biopsy every incidental nodule without risk stratification.

Part 16 — Adrenal Insufficiency

Primary adrenal insufficiency can cause fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, salt craving, abdominal symptoms, hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Central adrenal insufficiency may lack hyperpigmentation and mineralocorticoid loss.

Measure morning cortisol and ACTH appropriately and confirm with stimulation testing when the patient is stable. Exogenous glucocorticoids can suppress the axis; do not stop prolonged therapy abruptly without assessing risk and a taper plan.

Part 17 — Adrenal Crisis

Shock, severe weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or hypoglycemia in a patient with known or possible adrenal insufficiency is an emergency. Stress, infection, surgery, trauma, or abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal can precipitate crisis.

Obtain appropriate samples if this does not delay care, then give stress-dose glucocorticoid and fluids according to emergency protocol. The Endocrine Society recommends immediate treatment when severe symptoms or adrenal crisis are present rather than waiting for test results.

Part 18 — Cortisol Excess

Consider endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoid excess with proximal weakness, easy bruising, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, resistant hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, or adrenal features. Common obesity alone is not sufficient.

Exclude exogenous exposure, including injections, creams, inhaled products, and supplements. Screening tests are selected for the clinical context; random cortisol is not a general screening test.

Part 19 — Pituitary and Sellar Red Flags

Headache with visual-field change, ophthalmoplegia, altered mentation, hypotension, or acute endocrine collapse raises concern for pituitary apoplexy. Galactorrhea, menstrual or sexual dysfunction, growth change, or multiple hormone deficits may suggest chronic pituitary disease.

Evaluate the entire axis and urgent visual or adrenal risk. Treating central hypothyroidism without recognizing cortisol deficiency can be dangerous.

Part 20 — Sodium Disorders Reflect Water Balance

Hyponatremia requires assessment of symptoms, acuity, glucose, measured osmolality when appropriate, volume status, urine osmolality and sodium, kidney function, medications, thyroid, and adrenal context. Hypernatremia usually reflects water deficit relative to sodium or impaired access to water.

Seizure, coma, severe confusion, or rapid change requires emergency management. Correction rate matters because overly rapid shifts can cause devastating neurologic injury.

Part 21 — Potassium Disorders Affect Cardiac Conduction

Hyperkalemia can result from impaired renal excretion, RAAS-active medicines, cellular shift, tissue breakdown, or specimen artifact. Hypokalemia can result from GI or renal loss, diuretics, mineralocorticoid excess, poor intake, or intracellular shift.

Assess symptoms, ECG, kidney function, magnesium, acid-base state, medications, and trend. A critical compatible result or ECG change requires immediate treatment; do not dismiss it as hemolysis without urgent verification.

Part 22 — Calcium Disorders

Interpret total calcium with albumin context or obtain ionized calcium when clinically appropriate. Hypercalcemia can reflect primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, medications, granulomatous disease, and other causes. Hypocalcemia can reflect vitamin D deficiency, kidney disease, hypoparathyroidism, magnesium disorder, or acute illness.

Confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, severe weakness, tetany, seizure, or marked abnormality requires urgent evaluation. PTH-based reasoning helps distinguish PTH-mediated from non-PTH-mediated hypercalcemia.

Part 23 — Acute Kidney Injury

AKI is an acute change in filtration and often urine output. Compare baseline creatinine and trend, volume and perfusion, medications, infection, obstruction risk, urinalysis, and systemic findings. Organize causes as prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal while recognizing overlap.

Severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, metabolic acidosis, uremic complications, anuria, rapidly progressive nephritic features, or infected obstruction requires urgent specialty or emergency management.

Part 24 — Chronic Kidney Disease

KDIGO defines CKD as kidney structure or function abnormalities present for at least three months with health implications. Classify by cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category. G1 or G2 alone does not establish CKD without another marker of kidney damage.

Confirm chronicity and repeat unexpected abnormalities. Use both eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio for risk, monitoring, and treatment planning.

Part 25 — Albuminuria Is a Risk Marker

Albuminuria can reflect glomerular injury and predicts kidney and cardiovascular risk. Exercise, fever, infection, marked hyperglycemia, menstruation, and acute illness can cause transient elevation, so confirm persistent abnormality appropriately.

Do not substitute a generic dipstick protein result for quantified albumin when the guideline calls for UACR. Increasing albuminuria or falling eGFR may change treatment and referral urgency.

Part 26 — Kidney-Protective Management

Address blood pressure, diabetes, tobacco, cardiovascular risk, sodium intake, obesity-related risk, nephrotoxins, vaccination, and medication dosing. RAAS blockade, SGLT2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor strategies, and GLP-1-based therapies may have roles in selected patients under current guidance.

Monitor kidney function, potassium, volume, adverse effects, and sick-day needs. A modest expected hemodynamic change can differ from progressive AKI; interpret timing and clinical context.

Part 27 — Cystitis, Pyelonephritis, and Infected Obstruction

Dysuria and frequency without systemic illness suggest lower-tract disease, while fever, flank pain, vomiting, CVA tenderness, or toxicity suggests upper-tract infection. Pregnancy, male anatomy, immune compromise, stones, retention, recent instrumentation, or resistant organisms modify risk.

Infection plus obstruction can rapidly cause sepsis and requires urgent decompression, not oral antibiotics alone. Obtain appropriate urine testing and culture based on syndrome and follow-up needs.

Part 28 — Hematuria and Proteinuria

Confirm dipstick blood with microscopy when appropriate and consider menstruation, exercise, infection, stones, malignancy, glomerular disease, trauma, and anticoagulation. Anticoagulation does not eliminate the need to evaluate significant hematuria.

Proteinuria with edema, low albumin, and lipid abnormalities suggests a nephrotic pattern; hematuria with casts, hypertension, and declining kidney function suggests nephritic disease. These patterns may require expedited nephrology evaluation.

Part 29 — Stones, Retention, and Obstruction

Renal colic is typically severe and may radiate, but aortic disease, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian or testicular torsion, appendicitis, and pyelonephritis can mimic it. Assess pregnancy, infection, kidney function, solitary kidney, pain control, oral intake, and obstruction.

Fever with an obstructing stone, anuria, bilateral obstruction, solitary-kidney obstruction, uncontrolled symptoms, or AKI requires urgent urologic evaluation. Retention may be medication-related, neurologic, obstructive, or infectious.

Part 30 — Volume, Edema, and Diuretic Safety

Edema can arise from heart failure, kidney sodium retention, liver disease, low oncotic pressure, venous disease, lymphatic disease, medication, or local thrombosis. Assess weight trend, JVP, lungs, urine protein, kidney and liver status, and symmetry.

Diuretics can relieve congestion but may worsen hypovolemia, kidney function, sodium, potassium, magnesium, and orthostasis. Treat the mechanism and monitor response.

Part 31 — Obesity and Metabolic Risk

Use respectful, person-first assessment of weight trajectory, adiposity-related complications, sleep, medications, eating patterns, activity, stress, food access, and readiness. BMI is a screening measure, not a complete diagnosis of health or behavior.

Treatment may include intensive lifestyle support, anti-obesity pharmacotherapy, metabolic surgery, and management of diabetes, hypertension, lipids, sleep apnea, liver disease, reproductive health, and mental health. Monitor function, nutrition, adverse effects, and weight-promoting medicines.

Part 32 — Pediatric and Pregnancy Differences

Children have age-specific glucose, growth, fluid, dosing, congenital, genetic, and type 1 diabetes considerations. Polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, and lethargy can signal new-onset diabetes and DKA.

Pregnancy changes thyroid reference interpretation, glucose pathways, medication safety, kidney physiology, and hypertension risk. Severe vomiting, ketones, hypertension, electrolyte change, or kidney dysfunction deserves lower thresholds for coordinated evaluation.

Part 33 — Older Adults and Frailty

Frailty, cognitive impairment, food insecurity, CKD, polypharmacy, and variable intake increase hypoglycemia and electrolyte risk. Symptoms may present as falls, delirium, weakness, or functional decline.

Individualize targets and deintensify high-risk therapy when burden exceeds benefit. Preserve symptom control, function, safety, and patient goals rather than pursuing numbers alone.

Part 34 — Common Board-Style Traps

  • Using A1C despite a condition that makes it unreliable
  • Stopping basal insulin during illness in type 1 diabetes
  • Assuming normal serum potassium means normal total-body potassium in DKA
  • Calling every low TSH primary hyperthyroidism without free hormone and context
  • Starting thyroid hormone in central disease without considering cortisol deficiency
  • Waiting for confirmatory testing before treating adrenal crisis
  • Diagnosing CKD from one acute creatinine result
  • Treating a positive urine culture without a compatible syndrome or defined indication
  • Missing infected obstruction or nephritic disease
  • Correcting sodium too rapidly

Clinical Case 1 — The A1C Trap

A patient with anemia and recent transfusion has polyuria, weight loss, and repeatedly high plasma glucose but an A1C that is not in the expected range.

Reasoning: Altered red-cell dynamics can distort A1C. Use plasma glucose criteria and confirm as required while assessing symptoms, ketones, hydration, and diabetes phenotype.

Clinical Case 2 — DKA With Normal Potassium

A young adult with vomiting, deep respirations, dehydration, hyperglycemia, ketones, and acidosis has a serum potassium within the laboratory range.

Reasoning: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis depletes total-body stores. Emergency management requires serial potassium assessment during fluids and insulin.

Clinical Case 3 — Adrenal Crisis

A patient recently stopped long-term glucocorticoids and now has vomiting, hypotension, weakness, hyponatremia, and confusion during infection.

Reasoning: Suspect glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency with crisis. Obtain samples if this does not delay care, give emergency stress-dose glucocorticoid and fluids, and transfer.

Clinical Case 4 — AKI or CKD?

A patient with three days of diarrhea has hypotension and creatinine twice the prior baseline. The chart labels the patient as CKD stage 4 from the current eGFR.

Reasoning: This is an acute decline until chronicity is established. Assess perfusion, medications, urine output, electrolytes, urinalysis, obstruction, and response while preserving the prior baseline.

Clinical Case 5 — Infected Obstruction

A patient has fever, rigors, flank pain, vomiting, pyuria, and hydronephrosis from an obstructing ureteral stone.

Reasoning: Infection behind obstruction is a source-control emergency. Antibiotics alone are insufficient; urgent urologic decompression and hospital management are required.

FNP High-Yield Framework: BALANCE

  1. B — Baseline and body system: Prior glucose, creatinine, weight, medications, hormone axis, and functional state.
  2. A — Acute danger: Shock, mental-status change, arrhythmia, severe dehydration, respiratory compensation, obstruction, and crisis.
  3. L — Labs in context: Timing, trend, assay limits, glucose-A1C concordance, electrolytes, eGFR, UACR, urine, and acid-base pattern.
  4. A — Axis and anatomy: Primary versus central endocrine disease; prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal kidney disease.
  5. N — Name the syndrome and competing causes: Probability, phenotype, precipitant, medication effect, and can-not-miss alternative.
  6. C — Choose care and consultation: Stabilize, test, treat, adjust for life stage and organ function, refer, or transfer.
  7. E — Evaluate and educate: Response, toxicity, sick-day plan, adherence, complication prevention, follow-up, and return precautions.

Take-Home Summary

Endocrine, renal, and metabolic problems are disorders of homeostasis. Begin with stability and rapid glucose when appropriate. Confirm diabetes using the correct criteria and recognize when A1C is unreliable. Prevent and treat hypoglycemia, recognize DKA and HHS, and provide explicit sick-day planning. Interpret thyroid results as an axis, distinguish primary from central disease, and treat thyroid storm, myxedema coma, or adrenal crisis as emergencies. Evaluate sodium by water balance and acuity, potassium by ECG and excretion or shift, calcium by PTH-based reasoning, and acid-base disorders by physiology. Distinguish AKI from CKD using baseline and chronicity; classify CKD by cause, GFR, and albuminuria. Recognize pyelonephritis, infected obstruction, nephritic and nephrotic patterns, stones, and retention. Individualize organ-protective therapy to cardiovascular, kidney, weight, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, frailty, access, and patient goals, then monitor for benefit and harm.

Educational note: This lesson is educational and does not replace emergency evaluation, current ADA, KDIGO, ATA, Endocrine Society, urology, nephrology, obstetric, pediatric, laboratory, drug, or local guidance. Criteria, assays, medication recommendations, and crisis protocols change. Severe hypoglycemia, hyperglycemic crisis, adrenal or thyroid crisis, symptomatic electrolyte abnormality, anuria, pulmonary edema, infected obstruction, shock, or altered mentation requires urgent emergency care.
